global.headline: Trump expects Iran talks this week after rejecting Hormuz plan
summary: A day after rejecting Tehran's seven-day offer, Trump told Axios he expects talks to resume this week: "They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make." Iran's terms, he said, were ones Washington might have accepted a year ago. Qatari mediators continue shuttling.

Abbas Araghchi told NBC News Iran is "fully prepared for the war to be resumed" and would stand firm "even if it comes to a doomsday war", while keeping indirect talks open: "Diplomacy can never fail." The choice, he said, is Trump's. Iran still awaits a definitive answer through mediators, and Araghchi said UN ambassador Mike Waltz had not read the proposal; Waltz said Trump doubted Iran's good faith.
global.geopolitical: The public rejection did not close the channel: both sides now say talks resume while each insists the other must move. Qatar has replaced the New York corridor as the venue, putting a state with its own Hormuz exposure in charge of the text.
global.socioeconomic: Brent traded above US$106 and WTI near US$94 as Monday's Asian session priced the rejection for the first time, Iran having held to its terms. The strait stays shut, so Cape routings and war-risk premiums stay in force.

global.headline: Vucic resigns as Serbian president to run for prime minister
summary: Aleksandar Vucic resigned on Sunday, seven months before the end of his second and final term, after more than a year of student-led anti-corruption protests. Barred from a third presidential term, he can be appointed prime minister if his Serbian Progressive Party forms the next government after the snap parliamentary election on 25 October.

Parliament speaker Ana Brnabic, a close ally, becomes acting president pending a presidential vote. The parliamentary contest pits the SNS and its allies against Students Win, the student-led anti-corruption movement that grew out of the protests, and European Serbia, an alliance of pro-Western opposition parties.
global.geopolitical: Shifting the centre of power from the presidency to the premiership keeps Vucic in office through a term limit rather than against it — the manoeuvre used in Moscow and Ankara, now running inside an EU candidate state.
global.socioeconomic: Two national votes within weeks freeze decisions while Belgrade is still balancing EU accession against Russian energy supply. The protests that forced this began over a fatal station-canopy collapse, so public-works accountability is itself on the ballot.

global.headline: Gunmen kill 27 in two South African township shootings
summary: Eight armed men carrying AK-47 rifles and pistols opened fire on drinkers at a tavern in Wedela, on Gauteng's West Rand, at about 9.30pm on Saturday, killing 17. Roughly four hours later, at 1.46am on Sunday, gunmen shot 10 people dead at a shisanyama in Lwandle, near Somerset West east of Cape Town.

Police had made no arrests in either case by Sunday and had not said whether the two attacks were connected; there was no indication that they were. Investigators have given no motive and have not said how many attackers were involved in the Cape shooting. Manhunts are under way in both provinces.
global.geopolitical: Tavern massacres have recurred since Soweto and Pietermaritzburg in 2022 without a policing answer, and the pattern is now raw material for the contested foreign claims about South African violence that Washington has amplified this year.
global.socioeconomic: The targets are customers of informal township businesses, the trade with the least capacity to absorb a shutdown. What the AK-47s expose is firearm-control enforcement rather than the gun laws themselves.

global.headline: Swiss voters reject stricter neutrality in all 26 cantons
summary: About 70 per cent of voters rejected an SVP-backed initiative that would have written "perpetual and armed neutrality" into the constitution, barring Switzerland from imposing economic sanctions and limiting military cooperation with NATO to cases of imminent attack. It was defeated in every one of the 26 cantons.

The federal government and most parties opposed it, with Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis arguing it would harm national security and stop Swiss forces training with NATO. Support for neutrality as a principle remains at about 82 per cent in survey work cited during the campaign, so the vote separates the doctrine from its strictest reading.
global.geopolitical: Bern keeps the discretion to sanction Russia and Iran alongside the EU and to train with NATO. That removes, on a settled legal basis, the standing objection Swiss neutrality has posed to European defence coordination.
global.socioeconomic: Swiss banks and commodity traders avoid a constitutional bar on following EU sanctions, which would have forced a choice between market access and compliance. Geneva's role hosting mediation, Iran included, is unaffected.

global.headline: Seoul demands Ukrainian apology over disclosed North Korean POWs
summary: South Korea's presidential office demanded an official explanation and apology after Kyiv disclosed, in Zelensky's UN General Assembly address, that North Korean prisoners of war captured fighting for Russia had been transferred to South Korea — something Seoul says both governments had agreed to keep confidential.

Seoul said Ukraine went public without sufficient prior consultation and then denied any confidentiality agreement existed. Kyiv had itself asked for secrecy, arguing that disclosure would invite domestic criticism for giving up men it could have exchanged for Ukrainian prisoners; Seoul agreed on security, diplomatic and humanitarian grounds, including the safety of the prisoners and their families. It said trust between the two governments was seriously damaged.
global.geopolitical: The first resettlement of North Korean soldiers taken in Russia's war is now public against Seoul's wishes. That makes further transfers harder to arrange and hands Pyongyang a grievance it can press on the families the men left behind.
global.socioeconomic: Seoul is already refusing US demands for forces at Hormuz. A rift with Kyiv narrows the reconstruction and defence-industrial work South Korean firms had positioned for in Ukraine, the one growth market its arms exporters were counting on.

singapore.headline: Simba breach exposes NRIC and birth details of 23,549 customers
summary: Simba said the personal information of 23,549 individual customers was exposed in a breach it discovered on 24 September and disclosed in a notice dated 25 September, reported here on Sunday. The data included names, NRIC numbers, dates of birth, mobile numbers and email addresses.

No credit card or bank account information was involved, the telco said, and it has found no indication the data has been maliciously misused. Simba said it had resolved the incident, taken immediate action to review the security measures protecting its core infrastructure and systems, and is notifying affected customers by email over the coming week.
singapore.geopolitical: NRIC numbers and dates of birth are the fields that make impersonation work here, and they cannot be reissued like a card number. The disclosure lands days after CSA said it had shifted to hunting intruders already inside networks.
singapore.socioeconomic: The cost falls on customers indefinitely rather than on the telco once: this set is exactly what scam syndicates need to pass identity checks. Expect PDPC scrutiny of a mobile virtual operator competing on price.

singapore.headline: Singapore proposes a UN framework convention on AI safeguards
summary: Delivering Singapore's national statement to the 81st UN General Assembly in New York on 26 September, Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan called AI the "most urgent frontier" and said the world must establish common rules and safeguards quickly. He proposed exploring "the idea of a UN Framework Convention on AI Safeguards", and said an international institution may be needed to set common technical standards for AI as existing bodies do in other domains.

Because "the risks from AI do not remain confined behind borders", he said, states need shared rules of the road. Singapore has also joined the Finland- and Norway-led call for greater safety and security of frontier models, and used the statement to argue for multilateralism itself.
singapore.geopolitical: Singapore is proposing treaty machinery while neither Washington nor Beijing has signed the frontier-AI declaration — a small state bidding to shape the rules before the two largest AI powers settle them bilaterally, as their new AI dialogue suggests they intend to.
singapore.socioeconomic: A standards body of the kind described would give Singapore's regulators, already running AI penetration testing across government systems, a seat in defining compliance — which its data-centre and financial-services industries would then sell into.

singapore.headline: Share of Sec 3 students taking eight or more subjects halves
summary: The proportion of Secondary 3 students taking eight or more subjects at the G3 level has more than halved in a year, from 34 per cent in 2025 to 14 per cent in 2026. Those offering six or fewer G3 subjects more than doubled, from 12 per cent to 29 per cent, while the seven-subject group rose from 54 to 57 per cent.

Among students taking six or fewer G3 subjects, one in five also offers at least one subject at the less demanding G2 or G1 level. The G1, G2 and G3 bands map broadly to the former Normal (Technical), Normal (Academic) and Express standards, and replaced streaming under full subject-based banding.
singapore.geopolitical: This is the first cohort-scale evidence that full subject-based banding is changing behaviour rather than relabelling it. Families are trading subject count for depth, which is what the reform asked for and what its critics doubted would happen.
singapore.socioeconomic: Fewer subjects per student changes teacher deployment and timetabling across every secondary school, and narrows the tuition market's core product. It also reduces the O-level workload that has driven adolescent mental-health caseloads.

singapore.headline: Six to be charged over assemblies at Changi Prison, State Courts
summary: Police said six people aged 31 to 70 would be charged on Monday over alleged roles in public assemblies and processions held without a permit, several of them outside Changi Prison in 2024 and 2025 and one outside the State Courts in February 2025.

A 31-year-old man faces three charges of taking part in a public assembly without a permit, having earlier received a stern warning for similar conduct in March and April 2022 and for obstruction of justice. A 56-year-old woman faces two charges over assemblies on 22 and 29 November 2024; she was given a stern warning on 18 September this year. The man and four others each face one charge of assembling in a prohibited area.
singapore.geopolitical: Charges rather than the stern warnings used before mark a harder line, and the prohibited-area count targets the location — a prison and a courthouse — rather than the message. It follows the charging of a 62-year-old woman over six permit-less assemblies last week.
singapore.socioeconomic: The Public Order Act carries fines to S$3,000 for a first offence, so the deterrent is the record and the process rather than the penalty. Death-penalty vigils outside Changi Prison are the recurring setting.

singapore.headline: Haze cuts a half-marathon short before air quality eases
summary: Decathlon and co-organiser MetaSport cut the inaugural Kiprun Singapore half-marathon from 21.1km to 10km at about 3am on Sunday, race day, after readings reviewed at 2am exceeded their action thresholds. The 10km, 5km and Kids Dash distances were unchanged, the awards ceremony was cancelled and all categories were made non-competitive, with no official rankings or results.

The 24-hour PSI in the central region stayed in the unhealthy band through Sunday morning before easing, and by Monday morning air quality across the island had returned to moderate levels. PUB separately urged the public to avoid a long list of areas on Sunday because of flash-flood risk.
singapore.geopolitical: A mass-participation event was curtailed mid-organisation on a threshold set by the organisers, not the state. Singapore has no standing haze rule for sporting events, so each promoter writes its own trigger and absorbs the reputational cost.
singapore.socioeconomic: Refunds, cancelled prize-giving and void results fall on organisers who sell a fixed distance months ahead, in a race-events market Singapore has been growing. Runners who trained for 21.1km got a 10km with no recorded time.

word.definition: Concerning the end of the world, or final and ultimate events.
word.etymology: From Greek eskhatos "last, furthest" plus -logia "study of"; originally a term of Christian theology.
word.example: Araghchi answered Trump's rejection in eschatological terms, saying Iran would stand firm "even if it comes to a doomsday war".
